commands.name: harness

commands.name: harness-resume

commands.name: harness-start

commands.name: harness-status

commands.name: harness-stop

commands.name: subagent-task-tree
commands.description: Execute a multi-task implementation plan as a chained subagent tree — you are the parent controller; you spawn one manager per task; each manager spawns a planner, a plan-auditor, one implementer per subtask, per-subtask auditors, and a final drift-auditor. (user)

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify

commands.name: batch

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: built-in-browser

It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. commands.name: xlsx

This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and wants to stop using spreadsheets. They need a small tool that reads the ledger and shows where the money went. They want it both as an importable Python library (`import pennywise`) and as a `pennywise` terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python package `pennywise` (Python ≥ 3.9) that installs with `pip install .` and provides:
- a **library**: `parse`, `ParseError`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, plus an entry type with `.date`, `.category`, `.amount`, `.note`;
- a **CLI** `pennywise` with the subcommands `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add` and `export`, JSON output where the brief asks for it, `-` for stdin, and exit codes 0/1/2.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I can `pip install .` and get both `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` command on PATH.
2. As a user, I can `pennywise.parse(text)` my ledger and get entries in file order with typed fields.
3. As a user, a mistake in my ledger gives me a `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) with `.line` and a message saying `line N`.
4. As a user, I can get the total balance, totals per category, and totals per month.
5. As a user, I can filter entries by category (any case) and an inclusive date range.
6. As a user, I can run `pennywise balance|summary|list` on a file or on stdin (`-`), as text or `--json`.
7. As a user, I can `pennywise add` an entry. A bad entry is refused and leaves the file byte-for-byte unchanged.
8. As a user, I can `pennywise export` to CSV.
9. As a user, exit codes and stderr tell me whether my ledger is wrong (1) or my command or file is wrong (2).

## Implementation Decisions

**Layout:** `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no dependencies, `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`), `src/pennywise/__init__.py` (re-exports the public API), `src/pennywise/ledger.py` (model, parsing, aggregation), `src/pennywise/cli.py` (argparse CLI, `main(argv=None) -> int`), `src/pennywise/__main__.py` (`python -m pennywise`). Tests in `tests/` use stdlib `unittest` and must pass with `python -m unittest discover -s tests` (pytest-compatible too).

**Entry:** a frozen dataclass `Entry(date: datetime.date, category: str, amount: decimal.Decimal, note: str = "")`, exported as `pennywise.Entry`.

**Parsing rules** (decided where the brief left room):
- Lines are split on `\n` (and `\r\n` is tolerated: a trailing `\r` is stripped). Line numbers start at 1 and count every physical line.
- A line whose content is only whitespace is blank and ignored. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment and ignored.
- Every other line, with leading and trailing whitespace stripped, must match: `DATE` WS+ `CATEGORY` WS+ `AMOUNT` (WS+ `NOTE`)?, where WS is a space or tab.
  - DATE: exactly `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}`, and it must be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` is an error).
  - CATEGORY: one token with no whitespace; stored as `.lower()`.
  - AMOUNT: `[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?`. So `.5`, `12.`, `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are errors. Stored as `Decimal` of the literal text (so `Decimal("2500.00") == Decimal("2500")`).
  - NOTE: the rest of the line after the whitespace that follows the amount, exactly as written (inner spaces and tabs kept), stripped at both ends. Empty string when absent.
- Errors raise `ParseError(ValueError)` with `.line: int` and a message of the form `line N: <reason>` (e.g. `line 4: invalid amount '12.505'`).

**Aggregation:** `balance` returns `sum(..., Decimal(0))`. `by_category` and `by_month` return plain `dict[str, Decimal]`. Month keys are `YYYY-MM`. `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns a list that keeps the input order. The category comparison is case-insensitive, and both date ends are inclusive.

**Formatting:** amounts are shown quantized to 2 decimals (`ROUND_HALF_EVEN` is irrelevant because inputs have ≤2 dp). A zero result prints as `0.00` (never `-0.00`). One shared helper formats an entry line as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`.

**CLI:**
- `balance FILE [--json]` prints `1457.50`, or `{"balance": "1457.50"}` with `--json`.
- `summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]` prints `name  total` (two spaces between them), sorted by name (plain string sort). With `--json` it prints a JSON object built in the same sorted order. An empty ledger prints nothing, or `{}` with `--json`. `--by` with any other value is exit 2.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--until YYYY-MM-DD] [--json]`: filter, then a stable sort by date. With `--json` it prints an array of objects with keys `date, category, amount, note`, and `note` is `""` when there is none. A malformed `--since`/`--until` is an argparse error: exit 2.
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`: build the line text, then validate it by parsing that single line with the same parser. On error, stderr gets a message, the exit code is 1, nothing goes to stdout, and the file is not touched (not even created). The note must not contain a newline (that is an error, exit 1). On success it opens the file in append mode (created if missing). If the existing file is non-empty and does not end in `\n`, it writes a `\n` first. Then it writes the formatted line plus `\n` and prints that formatted line. It does not validate the rest of the existing file. Errors from `add` say `line 1`, the line of the entry given.
- `export FILE [--format csv]`: `csv.writer` with `lineterminator="\n"`, header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in the same order as `list` (date-sorted, stable), amounts with 2 decimals, note empty when there is none. Only `csv` is accepted (argparse `choices`), anything else is exit 2.
- `FILE` may be `-` for stdin in balance, summary, list and export. For `add`, `-` is an ordinary file name.
- Exit codes: 0 on success. 1 on a `ParseError`: stderr gets `pennywise: line N: …` and stdout gets nothing (build all output before printing anything). 2 on an unreadable or missing file (stderr gets `pennywise: cannot read FILE: …`) or on any argparse usage error (no command, unknown command, bad option or choice, bad date).
- Files are read and written as UTF-8.

## Testing Decisions

- Unit tests for the parser cover every rule above: valid forms (`2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `12.5`, `-0.99`), invalid forms (`12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `2024-02-30`, missing fields), tabs and mixed whitespace, a note with inner spaces, case folding, line numbering that counts blank and comment lines, and `ParseError` being a `ValueError` with `.line` and `line N` in the message.
- Unit tests for `balance` (including empty → `Decimal(0)`), `by_category`, `by_month` and `filter_entries` (each filter alone and combined, inclusive ends, order kept).
- CLI tests call `cli.main([...])` with captured stdout and stderr, and stdin swapped for `-`. They also run the real `python -m pennywise` through a subprocess for exit codes. They cover every example output in the brief verbatim, JSON shapes, stdin, `add` (creating the file, appending, missing trailing newline, refusal leaving bytes identical and not creating the file), export CSV, and each exit code path.
- One packaging smoke test: `pip install .` into a temp venv exposes `pennywise` and `import pennywise` (this may be skipped when there is no network or venv).

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies, export formats other than CSV, editing or deleting existing entries, currencies, budgets, a config file.
- Validating the whole existing file during `add`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` on Python ≥3.9 installs the importable `pennywise` package and a `pennywise` console script. There are no runtime dependencies.
- [ ] `pennywise.parse` returns `Entry` objects in file order with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal), `.note` (str, `""` if none).
- [ ] The amount grammar accepts `12`, `+12`, `12.5`, `-0.99`, `2500.00` and rejects `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`.
- [ ] Blank and `#` comment lines are ignored but counted. Fields may be separated by any mix of spaces and tabs. The note is kept verbatim apart from trimming its ends.
- [ ] Bad lines, including impossible dates like `2024-02-30`, raise `pennywise.ParseError` (subclass of `ValueError`) with `.line == N` and `line N` in the message.
- [ ] `balance` (Decimal, 0 when empty), `by_category`, `by_month` (`YYYY-MM` keys) and `filter_entries` (case-insensitive category, inclusive `since`/`until`, order kept) behave as specified.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with 2 decimals. The brief's example ledger prints `1457.50`.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines. The default is category, and the brief's example output matches exactly.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category] [--since] [--until]` prints matching entries oldest first, with a stable order on ties, as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends, creating the file if needed, and prints the line. An invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file unchanged (or not created).
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with the header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `--json` on balance, summary and list prints the JSON shapes from the brief, with amounts as 2-decimal strings.
- [ ] `-` reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 on success. 1 on a ledger or entry mistake, with the line on stderr and empty stdout. 2 on an unreadable file or a usage error (no or unknown command, bad option value, mistyped date).
- [ ] The test suite (stdlib `unittest`) covers the above and passes.

## Original request

- [ ] `pennywise.parse` returns `Entry` objects in file order with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal), `.note` (str, `""` if none).
- [ ] The amount grammar accepts `12`, `+12`, `12.5`, `-0.99`, `2500.00` and rejects `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`.
- [ ] Blank and `#` comment lines are ignored but counted. Fields may be separated by any mix of spaces and tabs. The note is kept verbatim apart from trimming its ends.
- [ ] Bad lines, including impossible dates like `2024-02-30`, raise `pennywise.ParseError` (subclass of `ValueError`) with `.line == N` and `line N` in the message.
- [ ] `balance` (Decimal, 0 when empty), `by_category`, `by_month` (`YYYY-MM` keys) and `filter_entries` (case-insensitive category, inclusive `since`/`until`, order kept) behave as specified.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with 2 decimals. The brief's example ledger prints `1457.50`.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines. The default is category, and the brief's example output matches exactly.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category] [--since] [--until]` prints matching entries oldest first, with a stable order on ties, as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends, creating the file if needed, and prints the line. An invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file unchanged (or not created).
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with the header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `--json` on balance, summary and list prints the JSON shapes from the brief, with amounts as 2-decimal strings.
- [ ] `-` reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 on success. 1 on a ledger or entry mistake, with the line on stderr and empty stdout. 2 on an unreadable file or a usage error (no or unknown command, bad option value, mistyped date).
- [ ] The test suite (stdlib `unittest`) covers the above and passes.

Wall time was about 18 minutes (21:53–22:11).

**What I checked by hand:**
- The output of `summary` and `list --category groceries` matches your examples exactly.
- `--json` works for `balance`, `summary` and `list`; `export` writes CSV; and `-` reads the ledger from standard input.
